key_facts: The Communication Workers Union says about 400 Royal Mail postal workers are leaving per week, up from about 330 per week before the DM26 delivery reorganisation was rolled out, from a workforce of 83,000.

DM26 is installed in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices; the CWU has told members to pause further roll-out until a plan is agreed, saying it works in about 500 offices but has significant problems in hundreds of others. Royal Mail says the roll-out is 90% complete and expects it to be running in all offices by Christmas, with 95% of addresses delivered daily across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out.

Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 head office and supporting roles by the end of 2027, and is hiring an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period. Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets.

key_facts: The ISE surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they are becoming 'more accepting' of candidates using AI during recruitment at some stages; the most commonly accepted use is writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.

EDF closed its graduate scheme early after receiving 12,000 applications, a 10% increase on last year; graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, per the ISE, and only 16% of surveyed employers use AI to screen candidates, while more than half plan to introduce it.

actors: François Yvon (CNRS, French National Centre for Scientific Research)
key_facts: In April, Google said people were translating one trillion words a month with Google Translate; direct sales of machine translation were estimated at $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

OKA, a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles, has published more than 10,000 AI-drafted articles, each checked sentence by sentence by a human translator. Its 2025 study of 119 articles found 27% of AI-generated text was still corrected before publication, three quarters of those corrections were AI-introduced errors, and 5–6% of errors changed the meaning of the original.

Specialists cite mistranslations in legal documents (e.g. 'Le demandeur' rendered as 'the requester'; 'Madame X, épouse Y' rendered as 'Ms X marries Y') and in medical dosage units (Greek μ rendered as 'milli' instead of 'micro', a potential thousandfold dosing error).
François Yvon argues that AI translation reliability is hard to make 100% because word choice is probability-based, and probably correct is not the same as correct.
importance_reason: Feature-style analysis of AI translation quality and its industry adoption; no direct market-moving event, though the translation market size is mentioned.

key_facts: A civil servant, Kashim Chowdhury, 55, from east London, is on trial at Southwark Crown Court accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies.

He is accused of holding five overlapping full-time public sector jobs between February 2020 and September 2023 and earning almost £350,000 overall, obtaining the jobs through alleged false representations about his employment status.

The prosecution alleges he wore make-up to a video call with his manager at the UK Health Security Agency in 2023 to appear ill, and that the make-up began to separate on his forehead during the call.

The prosecution says he exploited work-from-home arrangements from the Covid pandemic, told employers he had to care for an 'unwell' mother, and was signed off from some jobs for 'mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder' without giving the sick note to all employers. The alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra. The trial continues.
importance_reason: Локальная уголовная история о мошенничестве госслужащего; без прямого рыночного эффекта.

key_facts: The consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% for the month of September, putting the 12-month rate at 3.7%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday; economists surveyed by Dow Jones expected 0.6% and 3.6%.

Core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% for the month and 2.6% annually, compared with estimates of 0.2% and 2.5%. The energy index jumped 5.2%, with gasoline up 9.1%; over the past year gasoline is up 34.2% and fuel oil 74.2%.

The Federal Reserve approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years in September, a quarter-point move taking the target range to 3.75%-4%. Markets expect the Fed to skip an October increase and hike again in December.
importance_reason: Headline CPI above forecast alongside a Fed rate-hike cycle directly affects monetary policy expectations and bond yields.
market_link: Hot CPI and expectations of further Fed hikes pushed bond yields sharply higher and turned stock futures negative after the release; energy-driven inflation links the outcome to oil and gas prices.

actors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
key_facts: US inflation in the 12 months to September rose to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August, above forecasts, according to official figures released ahead of the midterm elections.

The increase was driven by higher gasoline prices following disruption to Middle East energy supplies linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran; crude oil reportedly rose from just over $70 a barrel before the conflict to over $100 currently.

In February the Supreme Court outlawed most remaining additional global tariffs; the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them. A New York Fed study found US businesses absorbed nearly 90% of the added tariff cost, with each percentage point of average tariffs raising consumer goods prices by nearly 0.25% after one year.
The Federal Reserve's inflation target is 2%; inflation peaked at about 9% during the Covid-era supply disruptions and the 2022 oil price surge after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
importance_reason: Inflation above forecasts ahead of the Fed's policy decisions, combined with an oil shock from Middle East supply disruption, has direct implications for monetary policy and markets.
market_link: Higher gasoline and crude prices and sticky inflation may keep the Fed from cutting rates, affecting bonds, the dollar, and energy equities.

key_facts: Waiting times for practical driving tests in the UK fell below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024; in September learners waited on average 19.7 weeks (about five months).

The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of candidates passing. The DVSA's earlier target of a seven-week average by the end of last year was pushed back to summer 2026 and then acknowledged as unattainable, with seven weeks now not expected until next autumn.

Earlier in 2026 the DVSA changed its booking system so only the learner can book a test, stopping resale of slots by third-party providers using bots. The DVSA says examiner numbers are at their highest level since November 2017.

A driving instructor interviewed by the BBC said recruitment of examiners is still insufficient and that in many areas the booking wait is 21 weeks; the government minister said the previous government left a record backlog.
